title: Interview Playbook
summary: Everything from the first minute to the last: how to run a 45-minute system design round and what interviewers score.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text: 3–5 core features. Say what's out of scope.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Scale, latency, availability, consistency, read:write ratio.

items.title: Estimation
items.text: QPS avg + peak, storage/yr, bandwidth, cache size. Only numbers that change the design.

items.title: API + data model
items.text: 4–6 endpoints, core entities, keys, the hot query.

items.title: High-level design
items.text: Boxes and arrows that satisfy every functional requirement. Walk one request end to end.

items.title: Deep dives
items.text: 2–3 hardest parts: hot path scaling, consistency, failure handling.

items.title: Wrap-up
items.text: Bottlenecks, monitoring, 10× scale, what you'd revisit.

blocks.title: Open with
blocks.text: "I'll start by pinning down requirements and scale, sketch an API and data model, draw a simple design that works, then go deep on the two or three hardest parts. Stop me if you want to focus somewhere specific."

head: Ask about
Example question
Why it matters
rows: How many daily users? Peak events?
What are the 3 things a user must do?
What's acceptable p99 for the main action?
Can users see stale data? For how long?
What happens if it's down 5 minutes?

items: Write endpoints as `VERB /resource` with the request and response fields that matter.
Name the **hot query** and design keys and indexes for it.
Pick the store after the access pattern: say why, and what you rejected.
Mention pagination (cursor), idempotency keys for creates, and auth in one line each.

blocks.text: Most designs start from the same skeleton. Draw it fast, then bend it to the problem.

blocks.caption: The default skeleton: add, remove and rename boxes to fit

blocks.title: Walk the request
blocks.text: After drawing, narrate one write and one read through every box. It proves the design works and surfaces gaps before the interviewer does.
Pick the deep dives that the problem's requirements make hardest. For each: name the bottleneck, list 2–3 options, choose with a trade-off, mention monitoring.

head: If the problem has…
Go deep on
rows: Caching layers, CDN, read replicas, hot keys
Fan-out on write vs read, ranking, celebrity problem
Upload pipeline, transcoding, CDN, adaptive bitrate

head: Signal
Strong
Weak
rows: Works end to end, every requirement covered
Goes two levels down on internals
Silent, or waits to be led

blocks.title: Level calibration
blocks.text: Mid-level: a working design with sensible components. Senior: drives the interview, proactive trade-offs and failure modes. Staff: frames the problem, reasons about evolution, cost, and organization.

items: "Before I design, let me confirm the scale so I don't over-engineer."
"The simplest thing that works is X. It breaks at about N QPS, so here's how we scale it."
"There are two options here. A gives us…, B gives us…. Given our requirement for…, I'd pick B."
"The bottleneck now is… Let me deep-dive there unless you'd prefer another area."
"If this node dies, … happens, and we recover by…"
"I'd monitor this with … and alert when …"
Jumping to microservices, Kafka or Kubernetes without a number that demands it.
Choosing NoSQL "because it scales" with no access pattern behind it.
One database box with no replication, backups, or failover story.
Spending 15 minutes on estimation math nobody uses.
Never stating a trade-off, a failure mode, or how you'd monitor.
Ignoring the interviewer's hints to move on.

blocks.text: Bring one real system into the conversation when it fits: a post-trade pipeline that must not lose or duplicate a trade is a perfect example for idempotency, exactly-once processing, reconciliation and audit trails. Keep it to two sentences, then return to the design.
